articles.title: EU sounds alarm over Trump diesel ban threat
articles.body:
EU sounds alarm over Trump diesel ban threat
A US ban on diesel exports could squeeze the EU’s energy market, which is already strained by reduced Russian supplies due to sanctions and disruptions in flows from the Middle East, officials in Brussels have warned.
European Commission spokesman Olof Gill told Politico on Thursday that Brussels was concerned by reports that Washington could halt diesel exports for 90 days, warning that any disruption “would risk negatively impacting both sides.”
The US has supplied about a third of Europe’s diesel imports this year, with its share rising to around half in August, according to government data. Prices at the pump have already reached record highs in Germany and the Netherlands.
Commission spokeswoman Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said Brussels was monitoring the markets and security of supply “very, very closely,” noting that the US was a “major supplier” of both diesel and liquefied natural gas as part of the bloc’s “diversification strategy since 2022.”
Trump backed the idea of restricting exports on Tuesday as US diesel prices hit a record $6.52 a gallon ($1.72 per liter). “I’ve said let’s not send out the diesel,” he told reporters ahead of a meeting with Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky.
Trump has also repeatedly urged Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, saying the attacks were contributing to a global diesel shortage.
The issue was raised during talks between Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in New York on Wednesday. According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, Lavrov said Ukrainian attacks on energy and cross-border infrastructure were deliberately contributing to instability in global energy markets.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to stabilize its domestic market. The measures run through January, although direct producers have been permitted to export diesel, marine fuel and gasoline since September.
Supplies have also been squeezed by the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a route that normally carries around a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. Gulf diesel and gasoline exports fell to just over a quarter of pre-war levels in August, according to the International Energy Agency.
The EU has sharply reduced purchases of Russian energy since the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Russia’s share of the bloc’s gas imports plunged from 45% to 12% by 2025, while its share of oil imports dropped from 27% to about 2%.
Moscow has blamed the EU’s decision to cut Russian energy imports as a key factor behind the crisis. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said last week that Europe was facing “the worst energy crisis in history,” describing the situation as “self-made.”

articles.title: Russian, Iranian foreign ministers say only diplomatic solution to conflict around Iran
articles.body:
Russian, Iranian foreign ministers say only diplomatic solution to conflict around Iran
Sept 25 - Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and his Iranian counterpart met on Thursday and Moscow said both agreed that only a diplomatic settlement could end tension in the Middle East sparked by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
"Current regional and international issues were discussed with emphasis on the situation around Iran," Russia's Foreign Ministry said in a statement after Lavrov and Iran's Abbas Araqchi met in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
"It was stressed that there is no alternative to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the illegal actions of the United States and Israel."
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian signed a strategic cooperation partnership in 2025 which provides for a deepening of bilateral ties and closer defence cooperation, but includes no mutual defence clause.
Each side has provided the other with military know-how and equipment.
Pezeshkian thanked Vladimir Putin earlier this month for Moscow's position on the Iran war and said together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism".
Pezeshkian said in an interview published on Thursday that it was up to the US to choose when the Iran war would end, when asked if the conflict could end by the end of the year. REUTERS

articles.title: Legislation among options to regulate minors’ social media use: justice minister
articles.body:
Legislation among options to regulate minors’ social media use: justice minister
Paul Lam dismisses concerns that measures could infringe on individual rights, saying goal is to protect children in Hong Kong from online harms
Introducing legislation to protect minors by regulating social media use is among the options on the table, Hong Kong’s justice minister has said, after the latest policy address unveiled plans to create a task force to review the situation.
Speaking to the South China Morning Post and other media outlets on Wednesday, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok dismissed concerns that such measures could infringe on individual rights and freedoms, emphasising that the goal was to protect children from undesirable content such as pornography.
His remarks followed Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu’s policy address on September 16, when the city leader announced that the government would establish a dedicated task force to look at minors’ social media use.
According to the policy address, the interdepartmental group, spearheaded by the Department of Justice, would review the associated risks of minors’ use of social media and artificial intelligence (AI) platforms, and assess whether legislative and administrative changes were needed.

articles.title: 'Not a coincidence': Opposition questions timing of Albanese's OpenAI hack reveal
articles.body:
In Brief
- James Paterson says the timing of the Medicare breach disclosure was "not a coincidence".
- The government is examining whether OpenAI could face legal consequences over the breach.
The Opposition has questioned the timing of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's disclosure that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics portal, as pressure grows for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence.
Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he did not believe it was a "coincidence" that Albanese revealed the incident while attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
"The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did," Paterson told ABC's 7.30.
"I don't think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City."
Questions around timing of disclosure
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Paterson, however, played down the severity of the breach itself, describing it as being at the "bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness".
He said Australians should be "alert but not alarmed" about the incident, noting the information accessed was not personal or private Medicare data.
It reportedly occurred on 18 June when an OpenAI agent tasked with researching public medicine spending gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.
The government says the portal contained aggregated health statistics and was separate from systems handling Medicare claims or individual patient records.
OpenAI detected the activity on 11 August but did not notify the Australian government until 10 September, when it sent an email to a Services Australia inbox.
Albanese publicly revealed the breach on Thursday after speaking with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman in New York.
The prime minister criticised both the length of time it took OpenAI to inform Australia and the way the notification was made.
Government examining legal options
The federal government has established a task force to investigate the incident, including whether Australia's existing laws and reporting requirements are adequate to deal with autonomous AI systems.
The review will also consider whether OpenAI breached Australian law and whether stronger penalties or liability rules are needed for companies whose AI agents cause harm.
Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Friday the government was examining what legal consequences could follow the incident, amid calls for OpenAI to be held accountable.
The government is also investigating whether activity linked to OpenAI agents affected systems belonging to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Victoria's Department of Health.
Calls for stronger AI safeguards
The breach has added to debate over how Australia regulates increasingly autonomous AI systems.
Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the incident demonstrated the need for stronger rules around transparency and incident reporting.
He told the ABC Australia could not be left "entirely at the mercy of foreign AI companies".
Nationals Senator Bridget McKenzie also called for safeguards to ensure AI systems were fit for purpose, telling ABC Radio National Breakfast that Australia needed to make sure "AI serves humanity, not the other way around".
The government has said it plans to develop national AI standards, with findings from the investigation expected to inform its approach to future regulation.

articles.title: Estonia imposes its own sanctions on two Russian oligarchs removed from EU sanctions list
articles.body:
Estonia imposes its own sanctions on two Russian oligarchs removed from EU sanctions list
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced this on X, Ukrinform reports.
Tsahkna said that on Wednesday, September 23, he signed the relevant order remotely from New York, where he was attending the UN General Assembly.
"Estonia did not support this decision and abstained from the vote. We will now impose national sanctions on both individuals. Russia has not changed course. Neither should we. Pressure through sanctions must continue to grow," Tsahkna said.
He emphasized that Usmanov and Fridman continue to support Russia's aggression against Ukraine and contribute to its continuation, which is why Estonia is imposing national sanctions on them.
Tsahkna also called on other countries to impose national sanctions on Fridman and Usmanov.
As Ukrinform reported, on September 22 the EU Council decided to extend for 36 months — until September 22, 2029 — restrictive measures against individuals responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. Russian oligarchs Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov were removed from the list.
France had pushed for Usmanov's removal, citing national-security considerations. According to reports, this came under pressure from Azerbaijan following the detention of two French citizens. Latvia, meanwhile, blocked the decision until the member states reached a compromise.
On Wednesday, Azerbaijan pardoned French citizen Martin Ryan, who had been accused of espionage and sentenced to 12 years in prison. This occurred one day after the EU agreed to remove Usmanov from the sanctions list.
Meanwhile, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius ordered the process of introducing national restrictive measures against the two Russian oligarchs after they were removed from the EU sanctions list.
Both Usmanov and Fridman are Russian citizens and were sanctioned by the EU following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Viral squishy toy trend putting children in hospital with burns
articles.body:
Squishy toys leaving children with burns as manufacturer asks Australian Border Force to help stop counterfeits
In short:
Viral squishy toy microwave stunts driven by social media are resulting in children suffering severe burns.
One manufacturer has asked Australian Border Force to stop counterfeits from entering the country.
Experts say most of the toys are safe if they are used as intended.
They are soft, often sparkly, a sensory delight and the current must-have for children around the world.
But what the viral squishy toys are made of is often not disclosed and a social media trend has put dozens of Australian children in hospital with serious burns.
Squishies are soft, squeezable toys usually made from a thermoplastic rubber outer shell and filled with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), maltose — a sugar-like substance — gels, beads and other materials.
They come in a range of shapes and sizes, from cubes to capybaras, and can be purchased anywhere from large department stores to small pop-up shops and online.
Demand for the toys has driven a rise in counterfeits that often do not disclose their contents, leading one manufacturer to ask the Australian Border Force (ABF) to stop them from entering the country.
Dangerous microwave trend
But even when the toys disclose their makeup and undergo safety testing, they are not completely risk-free.
A viral online trend has children microwaving the squishy toys, resulting in serious injuries.
A Sydney Children's Hospitals Network spokesperson said between January and September this year, 11 children were referred to the Burns and Plastics Treatment Centre at the children's hospital at Westmead for burns caused by heated squishy toys.
"Children were aged between 6 and 12 years old with burns ranging from mid to deep burns on the face, neck, chest, arms and hands," the spokesperson said.
"Some children sustained burns that required skin grafts and longer-term scar treatment."
Queensland Children's Hospital paediatric emergency physician Veevek Thankey said that, since April, he was aware of at least 13 burn cases linked to squishy toys being heated.
"The biggest issue that we've seen is actually the burns themselves as opposed to the actual reactions to the content that's present within these toys," he said.
He said most of the issues have been with burns to the hands or face, which require "intensive management".
Dr Thankey added that because the gel liquid becomes sticky, burns can occur extremely fast.
If an incident occurs, he said the most effective first aid was to remove any of the gel from the skin and place the affected burn area under cool running water for 20 minutes.
A Tasmanian Department of Health spokesperson confirmed its burns unit was aware of a small number of injuries caused by these toys.
Other health jurisdictions were unable to confirm if there were any reports of injuries related to the toys.
Counterfeit concerns
The sudden popularity of the toys has led to a boom in counterfeits.
It is something Schylling, the manufacturer behind NeeDoh, has taken extremely seriously, asking the ABF to seize counterfeit products entering the country.
William Valentine, the distributor of NeeDoh in Australia, confirmed it had taken steps to combat counterfeit products, including registering its intellectual property with the ABF Notice of Objection scheme.
"Counterfeit products don't just infringe on our intellectual property — they bypass the rigorous design, manufacturing, quality control and independent safety testing that authentic NeeDoh products undergo before reaching consumers," managing director Benjamin Halls said.
"That's why we take the growing issue of counterfeit toys so seriously."
He said they were also working with local counsel to identify sellers of counterfeit products and take appropriate legal action.
Consumer watchdog the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) confirmed it has been liaising with several domestic and international regulators in relation to squishy toys, along with online marketplaces and businesses.
It said there were mandatory standards regarding the levels of lead and other chemicals contained in products, and warned of consequences if businesses fail to comply.
Counterfeits seized globally
In the UK, the Office for Product Safety and Standards issued a recall for Samsons Cash and Carry Squeezy Dumplings after they were found to contain an excess concentration of benzene — a chemical linked to leukaemia.
Thousands of toys, including squishy toys, were seized in shops across North East Lincolnshire. Another 81 were seized from a retailer on the Isle of Man.
In the US, the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) has also issued a warning about counterfeit squishy toys, with 55 shipments of noncompliant squishy toys stopped at US ports, preventing more than 355,00 units from entering the country.
A professor of analytical chemistry at RMIT, Oliver Jones, said that while the unknown chemical makeup of squishy toys can be concerning, they were most likely made from the same materials.
"It's just that the manufacturing quality and the amounts [of chemicals] that might be left over in the final product could be worse if you've got one of these counterfeit ones that have been made at short notice without proper oversight and brought onto the market here," he said.
He said other qualities like the thickness of the material on the outside of the squishy toy and its robustness were also concerns for knock offs.
The ACCC recommends consumers avoid toys with strong chemical smells, weak seams, loose beads and leaking parts and to look for clear safety information including ingredient or material information.
However, Dr Jones said most of these toys were made at a quality standard.
"If you bought it from a reputable shop … and it doesn't smell and it's got listing of what's in it and so forth, I wouldn't be particularly worried as long as it's used in the way it's intended," he said.
"Even if it's like the best quality made toy in the world, if you put it in the microwave, that's an extra risk.
"And I'd certainly be a bit careful about leaving them in hot cars just to be on the safe side.
"We just have to be careful that when something does go wrong, then we learn from it. And if we can improve safety with better data on what's in the toy and how it's been manufactured, that can't be a bad thing."

articles.title: Trump highlights US-China ties at state dinner with Xi
articles.body:
Diyar Guldgoan
25 September 2026•Update: 25 September 2026
US President Donald Trump highlighted improving relations between the United States and China during a state dinner honoring his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," he said.
Trump framed the remarks as a reflection of friendship between the two countries, despite longstanding differences between Washington and Beijing.
During the dinner, he also presented Xi with a gift created by an American artist.
“In that spirit of friendship, it's my honor to present President Xi with a gift made by an extraordinary American artist, one of the greatest in the world and designed in personal collaboration with Melania and myself,” he said.

articles.title: Top Russian diplomat meets with delegates from Pacific island states
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 25. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met with high-ranking delegates representing small island nations of the South Pacific on the sidelines of the High-Level Week of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly, the Russian Foreign Ministry said.
"The sides held a substantive exchange of views on current international and regional challenges and discussed prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation between Russia and the participating countries in areas of mutual interest, including climate issues, fisheries, shipping and education," the ministry said in a statement.
The participants reaffirmed their commitment to stepping up cooperation across a wide range of areas, the statement reads.

articles.title: Urgent: Xi says China-U.S. ties come to another historical juncture
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Thursday that China-U.S. relations have come to another historical juncture.
Xi made the remarks at the welcome banquet held by U.S. President Donald Trump. ■
